title: German Family Minister and Chancellor Merz Clash Over Proposed AI Tax
summary:
Karin Prien, who serves as Germany's family minister and is a deputy leader of the CDU, told Stern that the state must tax revenue generated by artificial intelligence to prevent the concentration of wealth in the hands of a few. The proposal has created a political rift within the government, as Prien's stance directly contradicts that of Chancellor Friedrich Merz. The ruling coalition has not yet agreed on a tax base or rate, and no official bill has been introduced.

Other members of the cabinet remain divided, with Economy Minister Katherina Reiche ruling out a new tax while Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil has ordered three ministries to study the impact of AI on the labor market. The debate over AI revenue follows a similar push by France, which recently introduced a €0.055 per GB tax on internet traffic. Critics of the regulatory environment in Europe argue that such fiscal measures and high energy costs are contributing to a "brain drain" of tech researchers from the region.

selectedTweets.text:
❗️ Germany's family minister wants to tax AI, putting her at odds with her own party leader, Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Karin Prien, a CDU deputy leader, told Stern that if value is mainly created by AI, it has to be taxed, and that there is no other way.

The gains must not go to just a very few, she said.

Digital Minister Karsten Wildberger, also CDU, called on 13 October for taxing the extremely high revenue from AI to pay for overhauling the labour market. He quickly backed off, saying he wants growth from AI and is not talking about new taxes.

Economy Minister Katherina Reiche has so far ruled a tax out. Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil of the SPD has three ministries studying what AI means for jobs and tax.

The coalition has agreed nothing yet. There is no rate, no tax base and no bill.
